title: Psychometric Evaluation of the Korean Camouflaging Autistic Traits Questionnaire: Evidence of Measurement Invariance and Sex-Related Camouflaging Patterns.
abstract: Social camouflaging involves complex strategies used to navigate social challenges, which are increasingly recognized across varying levels of autistic traits. Despite its clinical importance in explaining diagnostic disparities, no validated measure exists in Korea. This study evaluated the psychometric properties and factor structure of the Korean version of the Camouflaging Autistic Traits Questionnaire (CAT-Q) across levels of autistic traits. A total of 1,079 Korean adults completed an online survey and were classified into high and low autistic trait groups. Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses supported a refined 13-item, three-factor structure (Compensation, Masking, and Assimilation) with strong model fit. The scale demonstrated good internal consistency and convergent validity, correlating significantly with social anxiety, depression, and interpersonal competence. Full measurement invariance was established across autistic trait levels and sex. The high autistic trait group, particularly females, reported significantly greater camouflaging across all dimensions. The Korean CAT-Q is a psychometrically sound tool for assessing camouflaging behaviors, with higher scores significantly associated with greater psychological distress. This instrument is essential for examining sex-related camouflaging patterns and fostering inclusive environments that reduce the burden of concealment in South Korea.Lay AbstractMany individuals, particularly those with higher autistic traits, use social camouflaging to cope with or adapt to everyday social situations. They often hide or compensate for their autistic traits to fit in with others. The Camouflaging Autistic Traits Questionnaire (CAT-Q) was developed to measure social camouflaging, but there has been no tool in Korea. We developed and tested a 13-item Korean version of the CAT-Q with 1,079 adults from the general population. Participants were grouped based on their levels of self-reported autistic traits. Our study found that this tool is reliable and useful. It successfully measures three types of social camouflaging: Compensation, Masking, and Assimilation, and it works well for both males and females. Females and people with higher autistic traits use camouflaging more frequently. This suggests that camouflaging can be an exhausting task to meet social expectations, rather than a simple choice. This tool provides a useful basis for future research on social camouflaging. Future studies using this tool can help us better understand the hidden struggles and find ways to lessen camouflaging. This research could help build a more inclusive society where everyone feels safe to be their true selves without fear of judgment.
